notes:
I've written notes below for most of Luke 12:31–59, but several verses are thin or missing. My tools stopped me before I could read everything. The full Enduring Word and Precept Austin pages cut off before reaching these verses, and Enduring Word's sermon page on vv. 35–59 had only a video. So most points below come from the short extracts that appeared in search results. Where I found nothing, I've left the verse out or said so.

**Coverage at a glance**
- **Where traditions differ:** The clearest split is on v. 59. Catholic writers see purgatory in the parallel passage, Matthew 5:25–26, which Calvin and the Pulpit Commentary reject. On vv. 47–48, Reformed, Baptist and Wesleyan teachers agree.
- **Not found:** Any Lutheran, Pentecostal or Orthodox comment on these verses. Nothing from the Bible Odyssey site, and only one minor NET Bible note. Nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching about vv. 31–34.

---

**v. 31**
- Steven Cole (quoted on Precept Austin) says we should seek God's kingdom and He will take care of our basic needs (Lk 12:31-34). He outlines verses 31–34 as a command (Lk 12:31a), an assurance (Lk 12:31a-32), an application (Lk 12:33), and an explanation (Lk 12:34). https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-12-commentary
- David Guzik's summary page: seeking the kingdom first is not one more item on a priority list. It means seeking His kingdom in everything you do, including work, marriage and parenting. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/
- Guzik also says Jesus told them to *replace* worry with concern for God's kingdom, because a habit or a passion can only be given up for a greater habit or passion. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/

**v. 32**
- Pulpit Commentary: "little flock" is another tender name for the followers grouped near Jesus. Having warned them of hard times ahead, He wanted to show how dear they were to Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/12.htm
- Matthew Henry: troubles may come, but they cannot come between believers and the kingdom. And if the Father is pleased to give them the kingdom, He will surely pay their way there. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_012.cfm
- John MacArthur (quoted on Precept Austin) sees the "little flock" as a small group inside the huge crowd. It included believers, some coming to faith, and perhaps some who would later fall away. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-12-commentary

**v. 33**
- Precept Austin, commenting on Jesus' similar command to the rich young ruler, says Jesus was not establishing a new requirement for being saved. The ruler's real problem was that his possessions "possessed" him. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-12-commentary
- Guzik: earthly riches often keep us from seeking heavenly riches as we should. He adds that most of us are afraid of poverty; we should be afraid of wealth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/

**v. 34**
- Guzik's summary: God wants our attention on His kingdom and His treasure, not this world's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/

**vv. 35–36**
- Guzik: if Jesus' followers are not to be greedy or anxious, their focus should be on His return, something worth giving our lives to. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/

**v. 37**
- Precept Austin: these servants stay up in the middle of the night to serve their master, and servants do not have a life of their own; they live to please their master. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-12-commentary
- Guzik's summary: ready servants will be so richly blessed that the Master reverses roles and serves them at His table. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/
- Pulpit Commentary: in the world to come, the watching servants would no longer be servants but friends of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/12.htm

**v. 38**
- Warren Wiersbe (quoted on Precept Austin): living expectantly doesn't mean idly waiting on a mountaintop. It means living in light of His return, knowing our works will be judged. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-12-commentary

**v. 40**
- Guzik: Jesus told everyone to be ready for His coming, which is the most important thing anyone could ever be ready for. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/
- Matthew Henry applies the verse to Christ's coming to each of us at death. That time is uncertain and will surprise many, because most people are unthinking. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_012.cfm
- Crawford (quoted on Precept Austin) links it to the rich fool: he was ready for this life but not for eternity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-12-commentary

**v. 41**
- Matthew Henry: Christ's words apply to everyone, but here He seems to show the apostles were especially in view. Each of us should ask, "Does this word belong to me?" https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_012.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: Jesus seems to ignore Peter's question but really answers it fully, saying even more about rewards than Peter asked. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/12.htm

**vv. 42–44**
- Precept Austin: the master putting the servant in charge of everything is probably a picture of heaven's rewards. Those who served faithfully here will have meaningful responsibilities in eternity. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-12-commentary
- Pulpit Commentary: the apostles, if faithful to the end, would receive special positions of rule in God's city. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/12.htm

**v. 45**
- Guzik: Jesus links readiness for His return with a life of love and self-control. "My master is delaying" goes with a low, fruitless life. Some grow weary or cynical waiting, This is exactly the attitude Jesus warned against here. If Jesus seems to delay, it is to rescue more people. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/

**v. 46** (who is this servant, and what is his fate?)
- Guzik: ready or not, the master will come. He will punish those who were not ready and denied His coming, and reward the ready. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/
- Pulpit Commentary: some read "cut to pieces" as meaning scourging, to fit the following phrase. But there is no known instance of the Greek word διχοτομεῖν being used in this sense. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/12.htm
- Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: being cut asunder was a known punishment in the East. "The unbelievers" means the unfaithful, hypocrites who falsely call themselves servants. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/12-47.htm
- The ESV Study Bible (quoted on Precept Austin) reads "a place with the unbelievers" as pointing to eternal judgment and separation from God. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-12-commentary
- Bob Utley (bible.org) calls it a figure for final judgment, even on those who claim to know and serve Jesus! https://bible.org/book/export/html/21309
- Bob Deffinbaugh (bible.org) takes a different view. He sees the place as hell, but the "cut in pieces" servant as unbelieving Israel, which would be scattered. https://bible.org/seriespage/way-wait-luke-1235-48

**vv. 47–48** (different levels of punishment)
- These teachers agree across traditions: knowing more brings heavier judgment.
  - Reformed: The Gospel Coalition says how much light and privilege a person abused helps decide how severe their punishment is. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/essay/degrees-punishment-hell/
  - Baptist: John Piper (Desiring God) says we aren't told in what way suffering will be greater for some, But we are certainly told that there will be degrees of suffering in hell. His application is not to waste the light God gives. https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/is-everyone-punished-the-same-in-hell
  - Calvin: the more knowingly someone despises the Lord, the heavier the punishment. Ignorance gets lighter punishment but is not excused. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-47.html
  - Wesleyan: John Wesley says much knowledge will increase, not lessen, his punishment. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-47.html
- Gill and Clarke both connect "many stripes" to the Jewish law limiting beatings to forty (Deuteronomy 25). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-47.html
- Coffman (on the same StudyLight page) is cautious. He accepts the principle but thinks speculation about levels in hell gives no real insight. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-47.html
- Ellicott thinks the words had a hidden reference to Judas. Benson applies them especially to ministers and teachers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/12-47.htm
- A BibleHub Q&A article notes that Tertullian and Augustine taught unequal torments. It argues "many" and "few" speak of degree, not duration, and that the verse gives no support to purgatory. https://biblehub.com/q/Does_Luke_12_47_imply_varied_afterlife.htm

**vv. 49–50** (fire and baptism)
- Guzik gives three possible meanings of the fire: judgment coming on the Jewish people, the power of the Holy Spirit after the cross, or the gospel spreading worldwide. He also notes that Jesus called His suffering a "baptism." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-12/
- Matthew Henry reads the fire mostly as persecution. Christ allows it as a refining fire for those persecuted. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_012.cfm
- Henry likens the distress of v. 50 to a woman in labor who welcomes her pains because they bring the birth closer. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Luk/Luk_012.cfm

**vv. 51–53**
- Light of Israel commentary: the gospel brings peace in the heart of those who receive it, but division all around them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-55.html

**vv. 54–55**
- Barnes: cloud then shower and wind then heat are regular patterns. So too Jesus' miracles, preaching and the prophets should have shown it was the Messiah's time. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/12-56.htm
- Matthew Henry: Jesus now turns from His disciples to the people, wanting them to be as wise about their souls as about everyday matters. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-55.html

**v. 56**
- Adam Clarke (Wesleyan) says the prophets and current events should have shown them this was the Messiah's time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-56.html
- Thomas Constable: calling them hypocrites means they did not want to see it in spite of the evidence. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-56.html
- Ellicott: it was "the time of their visitation," and they didn't recognize it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/12-56.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary says they watched the weather closely because it affected their harvests, yet were blind to the signs of their own times. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/12-56.htm
- MacArthur sees the nation as an example of wasted opportunity. https://www.gty.org/library/sermons-library/42-179/the-failure-to-discern-the-times-and-the-threat
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) applies the verse to reading the signs of Christ's return today. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-56.html
- Modern scholarship: the Expositor's Greek Testament thinks "hypocrites" is too strong a word for ordinary people and fits a Pharisee audience better. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/12-56.htm
- A NET Bible note says the word "hypocrites" appears in Luke here, in 6:42 and in 13:15. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=Luk&chapter=12&verse=56

**v. 57**
- Matthew Henry: while we are alive we are "in the way," and now is the time to make peace through Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/luke/12-56.htm

**v. 58**
- One commentator on Precept Austin says the judge here is God and the adversary is Jesus. Hearers must settle with Him before facing God's judgment. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-12-commentary
- Barclay: everyone has a bad case before God and should make peace while there is time. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/12-55.html

**v. 59** (where traditions really differ)
- Traditional Protestant reading:
  - Gill: a "mite" was a tiny coin. He cites Maimonides on a debt demanded "unto the last mite." https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/reb/luke/12-59.html
  - Clarke asks whether weeping and gnashing of teeth could ever pay God's justice, and says it cannot. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/reb/luke/12-59.html
  - BibleHub's study notes: Christ paid the last penny for all who repent and believe; those who decline His mercy will face the full, exacting cost themselves. https://biblehub.com/luke/12-59.htm
- Against universalism: the Pulpit Commentary rejects the idea that "till thou hast paid" offers eventual hope. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/12.htm
- Catholic reading (about the parallel, Matthew 5:25–26, not Luke itself):
  - Catholic Answers lists Matthew 5:25–26 as one of two passages where Jesus taught purgatory. It argues the small "penny" suggests a debt that can be paid, so the prison is temporary. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/did-jesus-believe-in-purgatory
  - Another Catholic Answers article cites Tertullian (c. AD 208), who read the prison as a picture of purgatory for lesser sins. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/is-purgatory-a-catholic-invention-no-way
- Reformed reply: Calvin (on Monergism) answers the same parable sarcastically. He says he'll yield only if the judge is God, the accuser the devil, the guard an angel and the prison purgatory. https://www.monergism.com/refutation-doctrines-purgatory-and-indulgences
